title: Hadges v. Yonkers Racing Corp. (1995)
summary: The court affirmed denial of substantive relief but reversed sanctions imposed without the required procedural safeguards and adequate grounds.
notes:
The decision illustrates both substantive and procedural limits on sanctions. It does not insulate lawyers from inquiry obligations whenever a client supplies a statement.

Hadges, a harness-racing driver whose license had been suspended and revoked, was represented by William Kunstler; the district court fined Hadges $2,000 and censured Kunstler, partly for failing to disclose a related state-court action, and the Second Circuit reversed because YRC's Rule 11 motion did not comply with the 1993 safe-harbor procedure (service 21 days before filing) and the court imposed sanctions without notice and an opportunity to respond.

sections.Parties: Hadges, a harness-racing participant, sought relief against Yonkers Racing; his lawyer also faced sanctions.
sections.Material Facts: The sanctions dispute involved statements about employment and dates in a prolonged dispute over racing access. Some assertions were corrected or qualified, and counsel had relied on information supplied by his client. The lower court also criticized counsel in ways that were not a substitute for identifying sanctionable filings and providing the required procedure.
sections.Procedural History: The district court denied the requested reopening or relief and imposed monetary sanctions on Hadges and a reprimand on counsel. The Second Circuit affirmed the denial of relief but reversed the sanctions.
sections.Issue: Were the sanctions supported by the applicable Rule 11 standards and imposed through proper procedures?
sections.Holding: No. The sanctions could not stand on this record and procedure.
sections.Reasoning: The court separated failure on the underlying claim from sanctionable conduct. It examined the reasonableness of counsel’s reliance on a client and the significance of corrections, rather than treating every inaccurate statement as automatic misconduct. It also enforced the amended Rule’s separate-motion and safe-harbor procedures and the requirement of notice. Personal criticism of counsel could not take the place of identifying the particular violation and applying the governing standard.

learning.why: The court affirmed denial of substantive relief but reversed sanctions imposed without the required procedural safeguards and adequate grounds.

topics.cp-certification: The sanctions procedure and reasonable reliance on a client’s factual account required separate examination.
topics.cp-notice: Counsel needed fair notice of the conduct asserted as a sanctions ground.
topics.cp-safe-harbor: Failure to follow the separate-motion and safe-harbor requirements mattered.
topics.cp-judicial-discretion: Hadges illustrates limits on sanctioning discretion, including the applicable Rule 11 procedure and the adequacy of counsel’s factual inquiry.
topics.cp-frcp-11: The case construes the 1993 Rule 11 amendments' safe-harbor and notice requirements.

mnemonic.rationale: A harness driver and a sanctioned lawyer
